The joint polarization of $W$ and $Z$ bosons produced in $pp$ collisions at a 13 TeV energy level is analyzed, utilizing 36.5 fb$^{-1}$ of collected data from the ATLAS detector. Individual polarization components of the bosons are isolated by examining their respective angular distributions. The measured fractions of longitudinal and transverse polarization for the $W$ boson are 0.29 $\pm$ 0.03 (statistical uncertainty) $\pm$ 0.02 (systematic uncertainty) and 0.71 $\pm$ 0.03 $\pm$ 0.02, respectively, whereas for the $Z$ boson, these values are 0.19 $\pm$ 0.02 $\pm$ 0.01 and 0.81 $\pm$ 0.02 $\pm$ 0.01, respectively. The joint polarization states of the bosons are quantified by examining the helicity amplitude contributions, measured as follows: $|\mathbf{00}\rangle$ 0.11 $\pm$ 0.02 $\pm$ 0.01, $|\mathbf{0\pm}\rangle$ 0.18 $\pm$ 0.02 $\pm$ 0.01, $|\mathbf{\pm 0}\rangle$ 0.

In the framework of 3+1 decomposition of general relativity, the total energy is split into kinetic and potential components, both dependent on the metric and its first derivative. We demonstrate that by redefining a new variable as the first derivative of the metric, the kinetic energy can be recast as quadratic in this new variable. This reformulation allows us to introduce a novel term, the Fabric tensor, as it only involves the second derivative of the metric. Consequently, the potential energy becomes linear in the Fabric tensor.

To ortholattices, specific topological structures known as D-topologies can be associated. The set of all such structures for a given ortholattice forms a collection called the dual lattice. The relationship between ortholattices and their corresponding D-topological structures enables the construction of a Galois connection between ortholattices and their lattices of dual structures. The connection reveals that a particular type of topological structure in ortholattices corresponds precisely to a specific type of algebraic structure, namely upper continuous ortholattices with specific properties.

We introduce a visual proof script generator for coq proofs, leveraging a visual proof assistant's proof script format. This is achieved by utilizing proof objects from coq and a custom-developed visual proof editor, CoqProofView.

We establish a limit theorem that describes the behavior of the average of the fourth power of the absolute value of Hecke cusp forms, which is near the expected value. This expectation, which is considered the Riemann hypothesis limit, has a conditionally proven bound that relies on the strength of the level of the form. This new theorem also provides insight into the distribution of the values of the L-functions, which is related to the spread of values of the 2nd power of the absolute value of cusp forms, which has been studied in the past.

In interior point methods, complex nonlinear optimization problems are linearized using techniques like Taylor series or complex numbers, resulting in multiple equations with multiple unknowns. These equations are solved using iterative algorithms such as conjugate gradient, which can be time-consuming and unnecessary if a direct solution is attainable. To address this issue, we propose a method to determine the presence of multiple solutions in various Krylov solvers by examining the basis vectors' interactions with the matrix, enabling swift and cost-effective solution of the optimization problems.

We have computed a next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order (N3LO) correction for the polarized gluon-to-gluon splitting function, specifically for the part of it that involves the convolution of a quark and a gluon, within the framework of the variable flavor number scheme. This correction has been calculated for the O(α_s^3) order and includes the five-flavor scheme, thereby extending the previous work on the N2LO for the O(α_s^4) order, as well as the work on the O(α_s^3) and O(α_s^4) orders within the three-flavor scheme, at various five-parton scales. This correction has been implemented in the CTEQTF fit, and it is anticipated that it will be useful for future fits that aim to incorporate LHCb spin-dependent data.

The AI community has been witnessing a growing number of high-profile AI system failures in their applications outside of the lab for the past few years. The AI Incident Database, a newly created resource, aims to catalog a comprehensive list of these real-world AI failures, which have been repeatedly reported across the AI news outlets. By providing an exhaustive database of these incidents, the AI Incident Database will serve as a valuable reference for researchers, enabling them to gain a deeper understanding of the types of problems that AI systems face in their real-world deployments and, in turn, develop more robust AI systems.

We've developed a precise Exact Renormalization Group (ERG) method based on the principles of optimization and calculus, which can be applied to any functional ERG equation. By formulating the ERG equation as an unconstrained minimization problem, we've derived an exact gradient descent algorithm that's equivalent to the Trapezoidal time-discretized Newton's method applied to an auxiliary quadratic minimization issue. This ERG gradient descent method is seen as a functional generalization of the ERG flow, which was previously shown to be an exact minimization algorithm for a specific quadratic minimization problem in [1]. We've analyzed the convergence of our method and demonstrated that it converges to a locally optimal solution, with the convergence rate being quadratic near this minimum.

In contemporary business process management, process models are employed to outline objectives and strategies, with various types, such as Petri nets and temporal logic, each serving a distinct purpose. The strengths of one model over the other lie in its ability to detect potential issues in descriptions, such as conflicts leading to unachievable goals. However, real-world applications often involve combining multiple models, introducing challenges in detecting conflicts and defining common criteria for feasibility. This paper presents a method for detecting conflicts in hybrid process descriptions, integrating elements of flow structures and temporal reasoning, and demonstrates its effectiveness through a concrete example in BPMN.

Quantum circuit verification is a crucial aspect of quantum computing, and current methods rely heavily on manual or tool-assisted processes, which are often time-consuming and error-prone. To streamline this process, researchers have developed a high-level language called Proto-Quipper-M, designed for describing quantum circuits. To ensure correct implementation, we have created a formal model of its underlying semantics, and in this paper, we provide a detailed account of its process-based behavior, and then prove that our model aligns with an existing stone-tableau interpretation.

The study of extreme values in systems with many variables has gained significant attention across various disciplines, driven by an increased need to analyze outliers in complex systems. Within the framework of random matrix theory, eigenvalues provide a prime example for studying these extremes. Our investigation reveals universal patterns of eigenvalue distribution across different random matrix models, supported by numerical evidence showing that the largest eigenvalue behavior mirrors the broader distribution patterns. These findings also validate the applicability of standard statistical methods for the largest eigenvalue, confirming its distinctiveness from the bulk of the distribution. This validates the use of generalized extreme value theory for the largest eigenvalue, in contrast to the Gaussian distribution that governs the bulk, and our analysis further elucidates the underlying mechanisms driving these distinct distributions.

Achieving ultra-high phase sensitivity in long-lived dipole systems requires a massive entangled photon state, which is challenging to produce due to the limitations of traditional light-matter interaction. A new method using the cavity QED framework allows for the creation of entangled photon states by leveraging cavity-coupled transitions, resulting in a long-lived photonic quantum state whose phase can be measured with exceptional precision. This approach can also lead to the development of optical phase sensors with improved performance over standard devices, as demonstrated through a model of a phase-sensitive detector utilizing cavity-coupled Raman scattering.

Assembling a genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a complex, computationally intensive problem, particularly due to the need to identify and connect numerous sequences in various organisms. To address this, a parallel algorithm has been developed to accelerate the process of generating continuous sequences in a cell's genome by distributing the computational load across multiple computers. This approach tackles two key challenges: identifying overlapping sequences and merging them into longer, continuous strands. By implementing these solutions using a graph-based data structure, the algorithm effectively minimizes memory usage and network communication requirements, ultimately reducing the computational time needed to generate a genome assembly.

A modified logistic equation, proposed by Latushkin and Stepanyants, is examined in this study. The original equation's solution often diverges from biological reality by producing oscillations beyond zero. The proposed variation incorporates a time delay dependent on the population size, a concept rooted in cell biology. The new model's solutions are found to be globally stable and positive, and a comprehensive analysis of its dynamics is presented, including conditions for the existence of stable zero and positive equilibrium points as well as periodic orbits.

The concept of data depth is increasingly being recognized as a valuable tool in statistical analysis, particularly for identifying the core characteristics of complex data patterns. In this paper, we introduce a point process depth measure designed for analyzing patterns of discrete events occurring over time. The depth is evaluated using a metric-based approach that relies on the probability distribution of the underlying point process, as represented by its intensity function. The chosen depth measure is the median, which we adapt from a multivariate distribution to the point process context by applying a transformation that maps the intensity function to a suitable space. The resulting Statistical Depth for Point Process (SDPP) is then used to analyze the characteristics of the underlying point process, as well as its associated multivariate process. The effectiveness of the proposed depth is demonstrated through various simulation studies and real-world data analysis, including the study of COVID-19 infection patterns over time.

A hybrid energy conversion system, combining electrical and mechanical energy conversion capabilities through superconducting magnetic energy storage, is analyzed in this research. Theoretical performance metrics such as efficiency, power capacity, and energy density are theoretically evaluated under various constraints including conservation of energy and the second law of thermodynamics. The study also considers a scenario with perfect energy and power transfer to identify optimal operating conditions and maximum efficiency.

The GEANT3 detector at the FRIB facility will be utilized to study Germanium isotopes near a neutron number of 40. This study will investigate the nuclear properties of these isotopes to understand their structure and how it changes. In particular, we will study double-$\beta$ decay, nuclear reactions, and radioactive decays to gain insights into the nuclear structure of Germanium isotopes. This will contribute to a better understanding of nuclear matter and its properties, which has implications for our knowledge of the universe.

To accurately measure the masses of unstable, light to medium-weighted isotopes, a new method utilizing the isochronous mass spectrometry technique has been developed. By combining this with a precise magnetic rigidity measurement, the masses can be determined with high precision. A significant breakthrough was achieved at the GSI/FAIR Heavy Ion Synthesis Facility, where the technique allowed for the precise measurement of the masses of 22 short-lived isotones ranging from 104Sn to 122Hg. Furthermore, a new world record was set for the 22Hg isotope, with a measured half-life of 0.47(4) seconds.

We introduce a novel technique for simulating lattice field theories using standardizing flows, a method that accelerates Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. By leveraging this accelerated approach, we can efficiently explore the field theory's probability distribution. To validate our approach, we apply it to one-dimensional and four-dimensional scalar field theories, as well as QED in four dimensions, where it outperforms traditional Monte Carlo methods in terms of statistical accuracy per unit of computational time.

A novel approach to structured text recognition is introduced, which incorporates regular expressions to guide the character-level recognition process. By defining specific patterns for particular text types, such as addresses or product names, the proposed method improves overall accuracy and reduces the need for extensive training data. Instead of relying on a vast dataset, the new approach only requires a smaller amount of data for fine-tuning the underlying model.

A theoretical model for the production of top quarks in proton-nucleus collisions is developed and examined. The cross-section for such events is calculated using a theoretical framework that incorporates eight distinct mechanisms, which are then compared in terms of their relative importance. The total cross-section is calculated and a theoretical prediction for the differential cross-sections in terms of final-state momenta is obtained. The results are examined for various energies and are compared to the potential capabilities of the LHC and its future upgrades, as well as the potential of the Circular Electron Positron Collider.

This research focuses on cross-domain text-to-SQL understanding, where previously acquired knowledge can be applied to newly encountered, unrelated SQL databases with minimal adaptation. Current approaches typically address this challenge by converting new database schemas into a universal format or pre-trained language models, but they often require significant modifications to their original designs or struggle with complex, nested queries. To overcome these limitations, we have developed an innovative approach that leverages the strengths of both existing solutions, combining a pre-trained model with a dynamic addition of database attributes as needed. Additionally, our method incorporates an auxiliary task to improve performance on cross-domain tasks, revealing that both database schema embeddings and auxiliary tasks contribute positively to model training. Our approach outperforms current cross-domain benchmarks and excels in related, single-domain scenarios, surpassing the state-of-the-art.

The LoTSS first data release covers 47% of the sky at a resolution of approximately 3.5 arcminutes and a flux density of 0.1 mJy beam$^{-1}$, enabling a study of radio sources in the frequency range of 120-168 MHz. A study of 100,000 radio sources in four fields reveals a correlation between the observed number density of the sources and their mean flux density within 100 Mpc. This correlation can be described by a power law relationship, with the exponent varying from -1.15 to -0.85 depending on the mean flux density of the sources. This indicates that more powerful radio sources are more strongly correlated with galaxies than their weaker counterparts. A comparison of the results with previous studies shows a discrepancy at higher flux densities, which may be attributed to a change in the relationship between radio sources and their underlying galaxies. A study of the sources in the three brightest fields reveals a flat angular power spectrum at scales larger than 10 arcminutes, which is consistent with previous results. This suggests that the sources are tracing large-scale structure on these scales. A comparison of the results with predictions from cosmological simulations reveals a discrepancy at scales larger than 20 arcminutes, which may be attributed to a change in the relationship between radio sources and their underlying galaxies. The high-dimensional rank regression model is a robust alternative to the standard L1 regression model, particularly effective in handling outliers. However, due to its non-smooth and non-convex nature, developing efficient optimization techniques for this model has been a significant challenge. In this study, we introduce a novel Adaptive Coordinate Descent (ACD) method, which incorporates adaptive sieving, to address this issue. By iteratively eliminating insignificant variables, the ACD algorithm significantly reduces computation time. Our findings demonstrate that ACD outperforms existing optimization methods, especially when many variables can be accurately set to zero.

The entropy generation rate is an effective metric for quantifying irreversibility in time-dependent processes. It has been demonstrated that for certain classes of time-dependent processes, a minimum bound on the entropy generation rate can be established. This minimum bound is characterized by a matrix that is independent of system specifics. This work expands on previous research by considering a broader range of time-dependent processes, including scenarios involving low-precision dynamics. Our analysis relies on an advanced mathematical framework that generalizes vector fields using non-commutative algebra.

In an effort to mitigate environmental degradation, Artificial Intelligence (AI) solutions are being implemented. However, these AI solutions themselves have significant carbon footprints due to their computational requirements. This study aims to explore the hidden environmental impacts associated with the adoption of AI for environmental benefits. To achieve this, a multi-criteria decision-making framework is employed to compare the environmental footprints of AI solutions and the computational resources they entail. The proposed framework incorporates both tangible and intangible factors, including social and economic implications, to provide a comprehensive understanding. The results indicate that the environmental benefits derived from AI may be overshadowed by the carbon emissions produced during their computation, thus highlighting the need for sustainable AI development.

Prescriptive procedure monitoring (PPM) is a key area in contemporary business process management that focuses on ensuring processes are executed as intended. Recent advancements in the field have led to a surge in research, yet a pressing question remains: what PPM methods should organizations adopt to effectively monitor processes? To address this knowledge gap, a systematic review was conducted to consolidate existing literature and identify areas for future exploration. By analyzing 39 studies from a database search, the review provides a comprehensive overview of current PPM research, categorizing it based on monitoring focus, scope, and performance metrics. The findings reveal that PPM research is heavily concentrated in the European region, with a significant emphasis on the North European countries. The analysis further highlights that European scholars predominantly lead the field, with a notable number of contributions originating from this region. The review also identifies a lack of international collaboration and a need for more diverse geographical representation in PPM research.

We have developed and tested a novel approach to estimate the errors of post-processed solutions for incompressible fluid flow governed by a generalized Boussinesq model that incorporates temperature-dependent fluid properties and anisotropic heat transfer. This approach allows us to estimate the errors of estimated solutions for various objectives in solving partial differential equations, including residual errors and errors introduced by approximating the domain, solution, and heat flux. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the estimated errors effectively converge to the true errors in both L2 and H1 norms for estimated temperature and velocity distributions.

Machine learning stacking is a versatile technique that combines multiple predictive models. We've developed a mathematical framework to address the stacking problem, taking into account both predictor and meta-learner choices. We've then adapted key stacking applications for network design and staff scheduling to this framework. To tackle the inherent computational difficulties, we've devised a model kernelization technique. Furthermore, we've proposed a meta-learner kernelization technique, which enables us to significantly reduce the size of stacking instances with minimal loss of solution quality. We've also integrated these kernels into a mixed-integer programming solver to achieve faster solving times. Experimental results demonstrate a substantial decrease in processing time for network design and staff scheduling instances, while maintaining high solution quality when applying meta-learner kernelization.

Social networks are characterized by triadic relationships that exhibit balance.
Triadic connections can also convey opinions, which tend to be consistent within
each relationship. This research explores the dynamics of both the structural
and attitudinal aspects of opinion-based balanced social networks, limited by
specific opinion constraints. By applying a preferential flip mechanism, which
targets dissatisfied triangles based on their level of imbalance, this study
investigates the equilibrium behavior of these networks, which exhibits two
distinct states: one where opinions are evenly distributed, and another where
most individuals hold the majority opinion.

We've found new, regular solutions for a type of energy function in three-dimensional space, which doesn't have any singular points and is consistent with Einstein's general theory of relativity. This energy function, when coupled with a massless scalar field, yields static solutions that are both asymptotically flat and free of singularities. These solutions can be applied in various contexts, including using a massless electromagnetic field instead of a scalar field, or assuming a different type of scalar field with a specific potential.

The temporal progression of RNA polymerase and nascent RNA production across a gene is examined in detail.
Using high-resolution imaging of RNA polymerases in living cells, we've gathered extensive data on gene transcription across various model organisms.
These observations reveal that the length of RNA delays within a gene are primarily determined by its linear dimensions, contradicting previous assumptions that accounting for gene curvature is necessary.
However, we've discovered that small variations in delay caused by increased gene width are indicative of the opening of the DNA double helix, which is essential for transcription.
To accurately model these phenomena, we've developed a two-dimensional delay model that outperforms existing three-dimensional models in terms of simplicity.
Our findings provide valuable insights into the fundamental mechanics of gene transcription, which may be influenced by the physical structure of genes.

Recent experimental findings on the nuclear nucleus 64Ni have been analyzed and are found to be consistent with a specific type of nuclear interaction, known as a monopole force, present in a particular theoretical model, known as the Interacting Boson Model. This interaction, when applied to 64Ni, results in a unified description of its energy levels, known as a unified systematics. Furthermore, a notable aspect of 64Ni is its presence of a unique phenomenon, known as shape coexistence, which occurs at zero spin. This shape coexistence is triggered by a force that drives spherical nuclei towards a deformed, or elongated, shape.

Chiral SU(N) gauge theories in four dimensions with Weyl fermions in the fundamental representation are being studied. These theories, involving $N_f$ flavors of Weyl fermions, denoted as $Q_i$ and $\tilde{Q}_i$ for each flavor, are being compared to a proposed dual description. The dual theory consists of $S U(N)_d$ gauge symmetry, $2N$ Dirac fermions in the fundamental representation, and $U(1)_R$ global symmetry. By analyzing the $U(1)_R$ symmetry, the study examines the theories' behavior at low-energy anomalies and determines their $R$-charges. The $R$-charges are constrained by a set of inequalities, which are then used to determine the theories' dualities. The study finds that only theories with $N_f \leq N+1$ flavors of Weyl fermions satisfy the dualities' requirements. The results are further confirmed by examining the theories' magnetic duals and by studying the $SU(N)$ and $U(1)$ gauge theories' $R$-symmetries. The study finds that the theories with $N_f \leq N+1$ flavors of Weyl fermions have a unique magnetic dual, which is consistent with the dualities' requirements. The results are further confirmed by examining the theories with $U(1)$ gauge symmetry, which have a unique dual description.

A linear complementary pair of group codes $(C, D)$ is formed when the direct sum of $C$ and $D$ covers the entire algebra over the given group ring. We establish that a linear complementary pair of group codes exists for any ideal in F$_p$[G] for a finite group $G$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that codes forming a linear complementary pair correspond to a specific type of duality in the code space.

In the field of AI, researchers often encounter complex optimisation challenges that involve finding the most likely sequence of events in a story or solving practical problems with constraints. These challenges are typically framed as constrained optimisation issues, which can be tackled using a specific function that calculates the probability of events and sequences of events. This paper proposes a simplified version of this function, which is based on the most likely sequence of events, to reduce computational requirements. This reduction in requirements enables the identification of the most likely sequence of events in a story or the solution to constrained optimisation problems in a practical amount of time, even for complex scenarios.

In the field of computer vision, detecting and locating dropped objects is a relatively unexplored area. Our research focuses on solving this problem by combining asynchronous audio and visual data. Our proposed method involves using sound to narrow down the search area and then using this information to efficiently find the exact location of the dropped object. As sound cues can be misleading, we developed an adaptive mechanism to weigh the reliability of different sound-based hints. Our approach was tested on a custom-built, 3x3x3 meter grid camera system, and we found that dropping an object into a smaller, sound-defined area significantly reduced the time needed to locate the object when compared to searching the entire scene.

We've discovered a universal pattern in research on dense suspensions, where shear thickening transitions follow a consistent, simplified set of principles based on the behavior of microscopic particles. This is the first time such a global scaling law has been established, providing a straightforward way to predict and understand shear thickening across various types of suspensions.

In March 2021, Venezuela faced its most severe power outage in history, severely impacting the nation's economy and daily life. This event was attributed to a combination of factors including an aging power grid, a lack of investment, and the closure of key power plants due to maintenance issues and fuel shortages. To analyze the hourly electricity consumption patterns during this period, we developed a statistical model based on a hidden Markov chain. This model was applied to data from 100 distinct cities across the country, and our results show that Venezuelan electricity usage during the crisis adhered to a daily cycle, with variations in consumption across different regions and time zones. Furthermore, our study highlights the significance of an early warning system for monitoring and managing power crises in the future.

We conducted a user testing study to investigate the impact of customisation on the effectiveness of Web searches. Our results show that tailored searches can negatively affect both the quantity and quality of relevant information retrieved. In our experiment, we compared the performance of users with and without customised search profiles, and found that the customised users missed more relevant information and rated the found content as less valuable. Additionally, we observed no significant difference in the time it took users with and without customisation to complete their tasks.

Recent advancements in code generation using deep learning have shown promising results, but current approaches struggle with generating code from visual inputs like design documents and flow charts. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel graph recognition network that can translate basic flow chart elements into Abstract Syntax Trees. By incorporating Advanced Graph Convolutional Networks, our model effectively handles graph data, outperforming traditional image-based and sequence-based methods in program synthesis from flow charts.

This text explores multiple methods of simplifying complex climate models through reduction techniques. Several approaches to model reduction are demonstrated using a simple framework, and their applicability to climate and other systems is discussed. The methods covered include methods based on invariant manifolds, model order reduction techniques, and methods involving spectral analysis.

High-temperature and high-density environments, such as those found in the ejecta of kilonovae, require accurate atomic data for the calculation of line opacity. These conditions are believed to have occurred in the merger of neutron stars, giving rise to the synthesis of heavy elements, including r-process nuclei. The relativistic effects on inner-shell electrons significantly influence outer-shell transitions in heavy elements, making accurate calculations essential. This study presents the line opacities for Au4+ and related ions, utilizing advanced atomic structure codes and a collisional-radiative model, and compares these results to previous non-relativistic calculations and observational data from a recent neutron star merger.

The gastrointestinal (GI) tract is a complex, interconnected series of organs, each playing a vital role in digestion and nutrient absorption. Accurately identifying and tracking the GI organs is essential for diagnosing and monitoring various digestive disorders. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have significantly improved the efficiency of GI region segmentation, a crucial step in gastrointestinal analysis. This article provides an in-depth review of the latest techniques for segmenting GI regions, along with their strengths and limitations. Additionally, we discuss the challenges associated with segmenting the GI tract and the future directions for research in this area.

Compositional analysis is a statistical technique used to study datasets where the variables are interdependent and form a closed set, such as percentages or ratios. It's widely used in fields like microbiome research, microbiology, medicine, biology, ecology, and geology. This study introduces an R package, 'compositionaldataassessment', which facilitates the evaluation of compositional data using diverse visualizations and linear algebraic methods. The package enables the visualization of ComCoPlots, which display the effects of one variable on others within a composition, as well as the associated variation. Additionally, it provides tools to calculate and analyze the effects of variables using the Multivariate Regression Shrinkage Operator (MRSO) method. By offering these features, the package supports the exploration of compositional data and the identification of variable effects.

A comprehensive review of the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity survey data reveals that it does not support the existence of a 'planet wasteland,' a hypothesized plateau in the frequency of small, rocky planets. By analyzing the detected frequency of planets with radii up to 1.5 times that of Earth, we found that the detection rate is consistent with the presence of numerous rocky planets that remain undetected. This suggests that the CORALIE/HARPS survey has the potential to discover a large number of additional rocky planets, and our analysis also provides an estimate of the detection rate for planets with masses up to 10 times that of Earth.

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in various applications, but their attention mechanisms are often opaque and lack clear interpretation. To address this issue, we have developed a novel, trainable attention control system that maximizes the mutual information between its output and the input features it focuses on. This approach, called intrinsic attention, is contrasted with extrinsic attention, which relies on external sources to guide the attention process. Through experiments on object detection and image classification tasks, we have found that intrinsic attention produces more consistent and stable results, particularly in the face of input perturbations. Additionally, intrinsic attention leads to enhanced feature extraction capabilities, as evidenced by the clearer separation of different classes in the latent space. Our analysis also reveals that intrinsic attention produces sparser and more selective focus on relevant input regions, as opposed to extrinsic attention, which tends to capture excessive contextual information.

If dark matter interacts with ordinary matter through a mediating particle like a photon or a quark, it could be compressed into a tiny, clump-like structure, potentially forming a "dark star" or a "nugget." We're investigating the properties of such dark matter, particularly its behavior under the influence of a scalar particle, and how it could be detected through its gravitational effects or through collisions with particles in the Large Hadron Collider.

Reinforcement learning methods have achieved significant success in various cognitive tasks, yet they struggle with sample efficiency. Inspired by the brain's reward system, RL algorithms utilize sparse feedback to guide learning, but this efficiency comes at a cost. The sparse nature of reward signals in many cognitive tasks poses a significant challenge for ALR algorithms, as they require large amounts of data to learn effectively. To address this limitation, we draw from the insights of neurobiology, as the brain's learning capabilities are not solely dependent on reward-based learning. Our approach combines sparse reward-based learning with Hebbian learning, a brain-inspired learning method that operates independently of external supervision. By integrating these learning mechanisms, we demonstrate the possibility of learning on many cognitive tasks with significantly improved sample efficiency, as shown by our experiments on 11 tasks, including 9 from the benchmark suite of the Decoupled Cognitive Toolkit.

This work delves into a specific class of nilpotent algebras with commutative multiplication, 
where a maximal ideal is categorized by its algebraic dimension, 
and a dimension formula is derived for two-dimensional geometric categorizations. 
Furthermore, a comprehensive enumeration and description is provided for 
simple modules of this dimension across all algebra categories, 
along with insights into the corresponding high-dimensional vector spaces. 
It is also demonstrated that this high-dimensional space possesses a 
notably intricate and distinctive high-level structural complexity.

High-speed jets from supermassive black holes, produced by active galactic nuclei, are a common phenomenon observed across various stages of galaxy evolution. These jets can significantly influence the development of galaxies and their surrounding environments. Research has shown that galactic black holes with active jets existed as early as 300 million years after the universe's formation. This implies that these systems may have played a crucial role in regulating the universe's cosmic microwave background radiation. To gain a deeper understanding of these early black holes with active jets, we conducted a study that took into account the universe's background radiation. This research found that radiative cooling has a notable impact on jet behavior, particularly in hot, low-density environments, where the temperature of the jet can rapidly decrease, thus affecting its momentum and energy. This effect is most pronounced in systems at the highest redshifts, where the mass of the black hole and the speed of the jet are both critical factors. This understanding has important implications for our knowledge of the universe's earliest stages, particularly in terms of how black holes with active jets may have influenced the development of the universe's large-scale structure.

We introduce a new class of non-kinetic gravity Lagrangians constructed from conformal curvature invariants, in the form of $I^n + B_n\mathcal{R}^2$, with $B_n$ being a specific polynomial sequence. For $d=2n-1$ dimensional spacetimes, the $n$th-order I-term is particularly significant as it becomes topological upon integrating by parts, rendering the accompanying $ \mathcal{R}^2$ term the sole contributor to the equations of motion. Consequently, we derive the equations of motion for this class of Lagrangians in $3$d, $4$d, and $6$d spacetimes, and investigate their linearized stability around Minkowski space, discovering that only the $n=3$ case exhibits stability.

A novel, image-based approach to registering volumetric data has been developed, which is particularly effective for low-quality, high-volume scans. The method relies on identifying and matching symmetry-based 2D features within individual slices, which are then used to construct a discrete 3D feature descriptor. The approach is volume-agnostic and can handle volumes of varying sizes. The method's efficiency is further enhanced by integrating the method proposed in 'Globally Consistent Registration of 3D Shapes' to ensure robust and accurate registration. The integration of this method with our feature descriptor enables robust registration, which is particularly beneficial in volumetric data with low-quality images. The method's performance has been demonstrated on various datasets, including brain scans, liver scans, and kidney scans, which are available on the Shape Matching website.

Our analysis of photometric data from the SDSS and PanSTARRS1 surveys, along with our own observations, of the eclipsing binary system SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, a type of cataclysmic variable known as AM CVn, has revealed several key findings. The system's light curves, derived from our data, show that the photometric and orbital phases are in sync, with a 40.5-minute orbital period. Our photometric data, combined with existing observations, have allowed us to refine the system's eclipse timings, with a 2-sigma uncertainty of 0.012 minutes. Our photometric data, combined with existing observations, have also allowed us to model the system's light curves, with a chi-squared value of 1.04. Our analysis has also revealed that the system's light curves are asymmetric, with a 10.5% difference in depth between the primary and secondary eclipses. Our photometric data, combined with existing observations, have also allowed us to estimate the system's geometric parameters, with a 30-degree inclination and a 1000 km radius for the accretor component. Our analysis has also revealed that the system's light curves are dominated by thermal emission, with a 1000 K temperature for the accretor component. Neural networks' typical approach to summarizing feature maps involves global pooling, 
which is generally seen as a straightforward and computationally efficient method. 
However, our research provides a fresh perspective on this operation by linking it 
to optimal transport theory, which offers new insights into its potential drawbacks. 
Specifically, our analysis reveals that global pooling can be overly aggressive in 
its transport of feature information, thereby potentially discarding valuable details. 
To address this limitation, we propose a new optimal transport-based pooling technique 
that preserves more feature richness. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficacy 
of our method in various tasks, including image classification, segmentation, and 
global pooling analysis, outperforming existing methods globally.

The classification of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) using spectral line emission has been a standard method for a long time.  However, recent research has revealed a correlation between the ionization source and the orientation of the AGN, casting doubt on the traditional classification system.  To investigate this, we analyzed a sample of 100 nearby galaxies with AGN, employing a multi-wavelength approach to determine their orientation through host galaxy ellipticity.  Our results indicate that different types of AGN exhibit distinct host galaxy characteristics, with type 1 AGN associated with more irregular galaxies and type 2 AGN found in smoother, more elliptical galaxies.  This trend holds true across a range of redshifts and is not solely a result of orientation bias.  Our findings suggest that the properties of the host galaxy may play a role in the development and orientation of AGN, and that the distinction between type 1 and type 2 AGN may be more than just a matter of orientation.

This research focuses on a specific class of flat rotational surfaces in the 4-dimensional Euclidean space, characterized by having a 1-type Gaussian map in a certain sense. By establishing a characterizing equation, we first identify this characterizing set, and then systematically solve the resulting differential equations to determine their solutions.

We examine the effectiveness of self-supervised depth estimation as a foundation for training a semantic segmentation model, comparing it to a more conventional approach of pre-training with a classification task. Our findings, obtained through a systematic study of various configurations, reveal that the depth estimation-based pre-training yields significant improvements in performance across a wide range of scenarios, surpassing the alternative method by up to 10%. Moreover, this improved pre-training method exhibits greater resilience to variations in training dataset size and demonstrates enhanced performance transferability to different datasets.

Concise textual summaries can effectively communicate key insights from complex data sets, making them accessible to a broad audience, including those without specialized training. Our new model, TCube, generates compact, coherent narratives from temporal data, regardless of the specific domain. TCube's performance surpasses that of GTCube, a leading model in the field, and demonstrates resilience to variations in training data, including sample size and domain. TCube's efficiency is enhanced by a novel two-stage training process, which optimizes both temporal and linguistic representations. Additionally, TCube's ability to produce grammatically flawless and contextually relevant content is achieved through careful selection of training data and a strategy that prioritizes accurate representation of temporal information.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider has made significant contributions to understanding the behavior of subatomic particles, particularly in terms of CP violation and rare decays associated with beauty mesons. By analyzing particle collisions, the experiment has made precise measurements of parameters related to CP violation and discovered new instances of rare decays. These findings have expanded upon previous studies and provided a deeper understanding of the fundamental forces at work within the universe.
On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that represent Gibbs states, both generally and under the condition of high branching.

This study explores the well-posedness of global solutions to a specific set of hyperbolic problems, where the coefficients experience a limited degree of increase, defined by the function $e^{C\sqrt{\ln t}}$. To establish this, we have developed a new approach to the Sobolev embedding theorem, tailored to an asymmetric Mikhlin-type operator.

We've developed a new approach to Japanese long short-term memory memory segmentation, leveraging sequence learning to capture recurring patterns in sentence endings that signal the start of the next noun. By applying this method, we've demonstrated its effectiveness in achieving segmentations akin to those produced by high-quality rule-based systems, without relying on manually crafted rules.

Developers frequently turn to Stack Overflow for assistance, often seeking answers to technical problems outside of the platform. This research investigates the external links that developers commonly share in response to these questions. We've developed a dataset consisting of 1.2 million external links shared by Stack Overflow users, analyzing the sources from which these links are sourced, the types of content they contain, and the factors affecting developers' choices in sharing them. We've also discovered that a significant majority of the website administrators discourage or prohibit the sharing of external links, yet developers continue to do so in a substantial number of instances.

The analysis of galaxy properties across the entire galaxy population is crucial for understanding the galaxy formation process. However, a significant challenge arises when combining data from multiple galaxy surveys, which often cover different regions of the sky and employ different instruments, resulting in inconsistent data. This problem is particularly pronounced for the galaxy population in the magnitude range of -16.5 to -19.5, which includes the vast majority of the population. In this study, we examine the effect of selection biases on the galaxy population by analyzing the distribution of the stellar mass of the galaxy population from the 2dF Galaxy Redshift Survey and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. Our findings reveal a significant difference between the two surveys, which cannot be attributed to the difference in the stellar mass of the galaxy population, but rather to selection biases. In order to overcome this problem, we develop a method to correct the galaxy population for selection biases, which involves comparing the galaxy population to a control sample. Our results show that the correction of the galaxy population leads to a more accurate estimation of the galaxy properties, which is particularly important for the study of the galaxy formation process.

This paper introduces the Climate Knowledge Base (CKB), a comprehensive semantic repository that encapsulates climate-related information, facilitating insightful discussions on climate change. As part of the Climate Knowledge Alliance (CKA), CKB is a collaborative effort by partners from industry, academia, and non-profit sectors, working together to standardize climate data and promote knowledge exchange. CKB's development is driven by a need to facilitate a common language for climate data, enabling seamless integration and comparison across diverse datasets. By providing a robust framework for knowledge representation, CKB supports intelligent climate data analysis and enables innovative applications in climate analytics. The paper outlines the rationale behind CKB's creation, describes its current state, and highlights potential use cases for climate analytics.

Clinical information extracted from unstructured patient records is highly valuable for various medical applications, including medical research and hospital operations. However, the utility of this data is often hindered by its domain-specific nature, with models trained on data from one medical facility struggling to perform well in another. This issue is particularly pronounced when there are significant differences in coding systems used across medical institutions. In an effort to address this problem, we have developed an event extraction system for symptoms that can adapt to new medical domains without requiring any retraining or fine-tuning. This approach leverages neglect-based generalization, allowing the model to automatically disregard symptoms irrelevant to a new domain and effectively handle cases where patient symptoms are coded using different systems across medical institutions.

In autonomous vehicles, the primary goal is to achieve safe navigation, which involves making key decisions regarding speed, lane changing, merging, and route selection. Research in this field has been ongoing for some time, with a focus on using deep reinforcement learning to enhance these processes. This paper outlines the fundamental principles of deep reinforcement learning and proposes a simple framework for testing and developing such systems in a basic driving scenario, which can be easily adapted for more complex applications, including lane changing and merging maneuvers, which are implemented using the simulator driving-scenarios package in PyBullet.

Inspired by the brain's computational efficiency, researchers have been exploring the potential of spiking neural networks (SNNs) to create more energy-efficient deep learning models. However, the inherent randomness in SNNs has hindered their ability to generalize well, a shortcoming that is particularly problematic for classification tasks. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel approach that integrates a unique type of SNN, the Precise Spiking Random Neural Network (PRSNN), which combines randomness with a novel error correction technique. By integrating the Bernoulli Gaussian Process (BGAP) into PRSNN, we have been able to ensure precise spike generation and achieve high classification accuracy. The results of our experiments demonstrate that PRSNN outperforms existing SNNs in both accuracy and efficiency, while also achieving generalization capabilities.

This research investigates the properties of strange quarks within a magnetic field and thermal environment, specifically focusing on their individual contributions to the free energy density. We derived equations for the free energy density and magnetic susceptibility of strange quarks with various masses and charges under influence from a magnetic field at finite temperature. We also explored the impact of these quarks' mass, electric charge, and the magnetic field on their contributions to the free energy density and magnetic susceptibility.

Our vision for personal computing involves leveraging browsers as smart personal assistants, capable of handling tasks across various devices and applications, while also managing data and software.

We've developed Pando, a web-based personal assistant that can be accessed from anywhere, and is committed to maintaining control over user data within the browser's capabilities.

Pando's functionality is based on a combination of techniques, including a feature-rich interface, a plugin system, and a method for integrating with external tools, as well a framework for building and processing language-based commands.

We've tested Pando's effectiveness by using it for a week and also compared it to other assistant tools, receiving positive feedback from users who found it more effective than the alternative tools we tested.

A novel adaptive framework for approximating nonlinear eigenvalues and eigenvectors is presented, with rational interpolation employed to predict eigenpairs based on known information about the eigencurve's behavior. The method involves selecting data points for analysis, with an efficient and targeted approach prioritizing points that provide the most significant contribution to the error in the approximation. The framework also features a robust algorithm that minimizes the computational cost by avoiding redundant calculations and enabling the reuse of previously computed information. The resulting approximations are proven to be reliable and valid, with the analytical bounds on the error providing an accurate measure of the accuracy of the approximations. The framework is demonstrated through several examples of eigenvalue problems, with the examples showcasing the method's efficiency and ability to produce reliable results in a timely manner.

A subset of intermediate β-shifts is defined as those β-shifts with a greedy expansion containing an interval gap, specifically when the basic intervals in β-expansion have varying β-power intervals. The main goal of this article is to establish the topological transitivity of these β-shifts with interval gaps in their greedy expansions. Additionally, an important finding is that any β-shift with an interval gap in its greedy expansion can be represented as a symbolic power tower symbol sequence, symbolically equivalent to a symbolic power tower shift.

Using the MaxEnt method, we've studied how quarks and gluons behave in an even number of color degrees in $SO(N_c)$ gauge theories, with or without a specific type of quark mass. Our findings show that for large numbers of colors, the massless quark scenario results in disrupted symmetry and the formation of quark-bound states, which aligns with predictions made by another theory. However, adding a small quark mass can prevent the formation of these bound states, resulting in disrupted, but not broken, symmetry. This dual behavior is unique to theories with a specific type of quark mass, unlike the behavior seen in theories with Yang-Mills without quarks or theories with quark mass.

Machine learning models, particularly random forests, have been widely used for their predictive capabilities in various fields. However, their high accuracy comes at the cost of being difficult to understand, a problem referred to as the interpretability issue. To address this concern, we have developed an enhanced attribution method called Disentangled Attribution Curves (DAC). This method enables the creation of clear and transparent explanations for model predictions by isolating the individual impact of each feature. Unlike existing approaches, DAC can generate more precise and consistent explanations, even for complex models with interacting features. Our research demonstrates that DAC can effectively interpret random forests and a related model called boosted trees. Additionally, we have created a framework for comparing the performance of different attribution methods and used it to show that DAC consistently outshines other methods in our testing scenarios.

Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a highly effective technique for developing collaborative artificial intelligence (AI) models, allowing multiple organizations to train AI models without sharing sensitive data. However, significant challenges persist in practical applications, including the need for secure computation, data processing, and communication infrastructure. To address these issues, this paper introduces Flatee, a pioneering framework that seamlessly integrates trusted computation environments (TCEs) to enhance the reliability of FL. By combining the strengths of both parallel and tree-based FL approaches, Flatee optimizes communication efficiency and data handling. Experimental results demonstrate that Flatee significantly outperforms existing solutions, achieving a 2.4x improvement in computation time and a 1.7x boost in communication efficiency.

The growing interest in autonomous driving technology has led to a surge in available datasets, enabling researchers to test their systems using existing data. However, creating annotated driving data is a labor-intensive process, and existing datasets may not be suitable for all studies due to their size or specific requirements. To address this issue, we have developed a system that automatically evaluates driver behavior from various perspectives, and can be applied to a wide range of driving scenarios. The system's modular design allows it to be easily integrated into resource-constrained embedded systems, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through a comparison of driver behaviors among experienced drivers.

In a microservices architecture, the system's behavior is highly dynamic and unpredictable, which poses significant challenges for performance optimization. The complexity of microservices is further compounded by the fact that their interactions are often opaque, making it difficult to trace the source of performance issues. The flexibility of microservices comes at a cost, as their variability can lead to a decline in performance consistency. The problem is exacerbated by the fact that the underlying resource allocation mechanisms in current operating systems are not designed to handle the needs of microservices effectively. The dynamic and nature of microservices requires a more intelligent and adaptive policy learning approach to improve their performance. The proposed solution, Timeloops, is a performance counter-based policy learning framework that uses reinforcement learning to develop a performance-aware call policy for system calls made by applications. The framework is capable of adapting to the needs of various types of applications, including those with short and long interarrival times, as well as those with and without clear temporal patterns. The proposed solution is shown to be effective in a wide range of scenarios, including a variety of real-world microservices benchmarks, which demonstrate its potential to improve the efficiency of microservices-based applications.

This research introduces a novel classification system for linear classifiers in even-dimensional spaces, offering explicit representations for each classifier. We establish a one-to-one correspondence between this linear classifier system and a specific group of transformations, then extend this result to linear classifiers within spaces defined by quadratic inequalities. Additionally, we derive a counting method for these classifiers within both merchandise and semi-definite spaces, ultimately applying these methods to count specific types of linear classifiers in convex polytopes, known as arrangements.

In recent years, the application of model predictive control in various fields has gained significant attention. The current work explores the potential of stochastic model predictive control to address uncertainty in system parameters, illustrated by a simulation of a mass-spring-damper setup. The results of such simulations can be utilized to generate a probability distribution, informing the predictive control strategy. Alternatively, the probability distribution can be sampled to produce a set of discrete states for optimization purposes. The study compares the efficacy of both strategies in terms of computational efficiency and the quality of the resulting control actions.

This research introduces two innovative algorithms for identifying individual components in a mixture of matrices, where each component shares a distinct and low-dimensional structure. Building on existing methods, we enhance the separation process by integrating non-convex constraints into an alternating minimization framework, resulting in more accurate identification of the matrices. Under certain conditions, we demonstrate that this approach guarantees a unique solution and establish an established relationship with $\ell_1$-minimization. Furthermore, we develop a more efficient algorithm by removing Convex Optimization Problems from the computation, which significantly reduces its complexity.

A mathematical model describing population dynamics in discrete space under the influence of random disturbances is examined. This examination focuses on a scenario where two competing species experience different levels of random movement. The trade-off between colonization and competition is represented by the fact that more mobile species have an advantage in dispersing but are more susceptible to random movement effects. The study reveals that in the presence of random influences, the relationship between competition ability and mobility is more significant, with the more competitive species typically outperforming the less mobile species. However, under certain conditions, the less competitive species with high mobility can exclude the more dominant species. The study also investigates the impact of random influences on population distribution patterns.

In a d-dimensional abelian quantum double state of a group G, we identify the category of local algebras with continuous support as equivalent to the category of semi-simple G-bundles with continuous fibers and algebraic structures on a closed n-dimensional submanifold of the n-dimensional torus. A key aspect of our analysis involves developing a theory of groups operating on real continuous functions and defining algebras with continuous elements.

The interplay between magnons, photons, and phonons in cavity magnomechanics has been explored in depth. A key aspect of this system involves the entanglement generated between a magnomechanical mode and cavity photon, which has been enhanced through coherent feedback mechanisms. This study delves into the role of coherent feedback in amplifying magnon-phonic and magnon-cavity entanglement. A crucial finding is that the entanglement produced in these interactions is more pronounced than that in photon-magnon or phonon-magnon interactions. Moreover, the cavity's presence is pivotal in enhancing magnon-phonic interactions. A notable aspect of this system involves the ability to sustain magnon-phonic entanglement over time, which is facilitated by coherent feedback mechanisms. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced when the system is coupled with an external bath. A crucial factor in amplifying magnon-phonic interactions involves the coupling rate between the magnon and phonon, which is more pronounced when the coupling rate is in the range of 0.5 to 1. A key aspect of this system involves the ability to control the system's dynamics through coherent feedback mechanisms, which is particularly useful in controlling the system's entanglement properties. This phenomenon is particularly useful in controlling the system's entanglement in the presence of an external bath. We've compiled corrected one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for QCD, 
including all missing higher-order terms from the previous dimensionally-regulated calculation.
The compilation encompasses corrections to all relevant color representations and flavors, 
as well as higher-order terms associated with operator mixing and mass effects.
This comprehensive set of building blocks will be essential in constructing next-to-next-to-next-to leading order parton distribution functions through iterative spectral decomposition methods.

We present a constructive version of Neron Desingularization, specifically for one-dimensional local rings. This is based on a revised proof of the Neron Desingularization, which we adapt to a specific case. Furthermore, we develop an effective method for calculating integral closures in one-dimensional local rings that have minimal numerical complexity. This integral computation then facilitates the Neron Desingularization.

Historical sundials in Indonesia are being documented through a collaborative initiative by scientists and the public, focusing on preserving these timepieces that are often found in outdoor settings across the country. A comprehensive database is being created to preserve sundial information, which will serve as a valuable resource for researchers and the public, who can access a wide range of data, including a wide range of sundials, through a shared platform.

This research introduces a new integrated data and energy communication system that incorporates D2D technology, along with a reflective surface. By combining a low-power D2D mode and a D2D high-power mode, the proposed model optimizes energy consumption for low-power devices and ensures reliable data transmission. Introducing a reflective surface into the network enables it to adapt its state to the users' needs, thereby enhancing the overall energy efficiency. A cognitive reflecting surface is used to dynamically adjust its properties based on the users' requirements, thereby achieving a better balance between data transmission and energy consumption.

A new single-probe Laser Doppler Velocimetry (LDV) setup has been developed to map the 2D velocity field in a plane. This innovative approach utilizes one probe positioned at the intersection of two LDV beams to track particle velocities in the flow. By strategically placing the probe, a vertical and horizontal plane of velocities can be obtained. This technique has been successfully demonstrated in a simple channel flow, validating its effectiveness. Notably, this method offers a significant advantage over traditional approaches by reducing the equipment footprint, making it an attractive option for measuring complex flows in confined spaces.

We examine the complexity of deciding the uniform $1$-existence and $1$-universality problems for first-order sentences with a specific set of binary relations, finding that these problems are recursively unsolvable in this context. In contrast, the corresponding problems for first-order sentences with a single non-binary relation remain recursively solvable.

The performance of a transmission electron microscope (TEM) can be significantly hampered by magnetic lens imperfections, which can be quantified using an ellipticity index. In our study, we investigated the effect of ellipticity on the TEM's resolution and found that a programmable phase plate can be utilized to correct for lens imperfections, thereby restoring the transmission electron beam's symmetry. The optimal correction is achieved when the electron energy distribution's radius is minimized. The optimal correction conditions are influenced by the electron energy distribution, which is in turn affected by the microscope's lenses and their ellipticity. The optimal correction is lens- and instrument-specific, and can be found by adjusting the lens currents to achieve the desired ellipticity correction.

The concept of "computation" is explored through a phenomenological lens, focusing on its role as a tool for problem-solving and value creation. The assessment of a problem-solving method as a form of computation is established by two essential criteria: input flexibility and output adaptability. The article subsequently examines the underlying mechanisms of computation and its capacity to drive innovation, utilizing the assessability criteria outlined previously. The analysis is grounded in a broader understanding of computation that encompasses both biological and artificial systems, thereby expanding its scope beyond traditional technological definitions.

We are examining a simple random walk on a d-dimensional integer lattice, starting at the origin. For a given radius R, we want to calculate the probability that the walk will be within a certain distance from the origin after 2n steps, specifically if it's within a certain number of steps (k) from the origin. This probability can be broken down into two parts: the probability that the walk will take an even number of steps (2m) and be within that many steps from the origin, and the probability that the walk will take an odd number of steps (2m+1) and be within that many steps from the origin. 

To make the calculation more manageable, we're focusing on the case where n is much larger than R. In this scenario, our goal is to find an accurate approximation of these probabilities. 

To achieve this, we're using an approach that involves applying the CLT to a sum of independent and identically distributed random variables that represent the steps of the walk. This will give us a more precise understanding of the probabilities and will ultimately lead to a accurate approximation of the probabilities in question.

A new approach to understanding the central region of a black hole is proposed, based on a specific interpretation of the polymer modified Schwarzschild black hole model. By applying a coordinate transformation, we can recast the line element in a form that is regular throughout all spacetime. This allows us to define a global, light-cone-like coordinate system, in which we can study the properties of geodesics and their relationship to the structure of spacetime. Furthermore, we find that the equation governing wave oscillations can be expressed as a Schrödinger-like equation with a potential that is regular everywhere. This model exhibits a quasinormal spectrum, and we find that it agrees with previously proposed polymer models.

We have derived a general formula for the thermal energy storage capacity of A-B type two-dimensional crystal lattices with non-parabolic energy patterns, applying specifically to doped graphene. Applying this formula to graphene at finite temperatures reveals that its storage capacity storage capacity behaves differently based on temperature: at low temperatures, its capacity increases in proportion to the fifth power of the temperature, whereas at high temperatures, its capacity increases in proportion to the temperature's third power, aligning with the expected behavior for three-dimensional materials.

Our proposed MaskedSpeech system utilizes a transformer-based architecture to generate coherent speech on a sentence-by-sentence basis. To tackle the challenge of maintaining contextual integrity, we introduce a progressive strategy that temporarily hides each sentence in a sequence, forcing the model to rely solely on prior sentences for speech generation.

We've developed a novel approach for obtaining predictive intervals by projecting the latent variables of variational autoencoders into the original data domain. Our method addresses the limitations of existing projection predictive estimation (PPE) techniques, which are hindered by the Markov property in variational autoencoders. Our approach surpasses the predictive performance of PPE and the original data likelihood, particularly in scenarios where the latter is unbounded. We've also developed a computationally efficient algorithm for PPE, enabling its practical application.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have led to a surge in its application across various domains, such as computer vision and natural language processing. However, the complexity of these models has created vulnerabilities that can be exploited by malicious actors, who may gain control of the machine learning pipeline and manipulate its outcomes. This raises concerns about the potential for malicious influence on the training and inference stages of these models. This research focuses on a new type of attack, where an adversary, who controls an intermediary stage in the deep learning pipeline, attempts to manipulate the output of a classification model. To this end, we have developed two innovative attack strategies - one that relies on the adversary's ability to analyze input data and another that relies on pre-trained generative models. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of these attacks, which outperform existing attack methods in various scenarios.

Climate change is a pressing global issue, yet many individuals remain unaware of its severity or dismiss the scientific consensus. Research indicates that a significant portion of the population struggles to grasp the scientific process, while social media platforms have become breeding grounds for debunked climate change narratives. These platforms can distort public perception, with some people actively opposing the scientific consensus. A study was conducted to examine the prevalence of four prominent climate change conspiracy theories on social media, revealing that these messages are widely disseminated and can significantly impact public opinion.

A search for dark matter associated with top quark production is conducted using proton-proton collision data, collected between 2016 and 2018 at 13 TeV by the CDF detector at the LHC. The data amount to 137 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity. The data are analyzed using two distinct channels, one involving a top quark and one involving a pair of top quarks. The expected outcomes are compared to observed results in channels featuring multiple jets and significant missing transverse momentum. The results are in accordance with the SM predictions and do not deviate from them. The findings are used to establish new upper limits on the production cross-sections of dark matter in association with top quarks. The limits are set within the context of simplified models and are used to constrain the parameters of vector and axial vector mediators, as well as scalar and pseudoscalar mediators.

In this paper, we introduce a concept of Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality for n-extrangulated categories, and under this duality exists, we prove the presence of n-extrangulated structures within the left and right approximation categories.

We've developed a statistical framework for analyzing causal relationships in situations where treatments have distinct characteristics. This framework addresses challenges in estimating cause and effect when treatments are categorized and when control factors have an impact on different cause effects. To overcome these challenges, we've identified new criteria for cause and effect estimation, which rely on the relationship between cause effects and the way they're perceived. These criteria enable us to compare the impact of various treatment options. As a result, we can examine the impact of various fields of study on students' choice of careers. To do this, we've developed a model that takes into account students' preferences for various careers and their fields of study. Using this model, we've found that fields of study have a significant impact on career choices, with some fields having a positive impact and others having a negative impact.

High-quality antineutrons and hyperons can be created in large quantities using advanced techniques that combine nuclear emulsion technology with particle physics. These methods, utilizing super $J/\psi$ decays, enable researchers to study these elusive particles in intricate experiments. As a result, new, highly sensitive experiments involving antigravity, nuclear physics, and particle physics can be conducted with greater precision.
